1h5h4va: The system is the same as for -ar: you remove **-er** or **-ir** and add the ending. The typical vowel now is **e**: com**o**, com**es**, com**e**, com**en**.
sdv8da: Verbs in **-er** and **-ir** differ only in **nosotros** and **vosotros**: com**emos** / viv**imos**, com**éis** / viv**ís**. In all other persons they are the same: com**e** / viv**e**.

104bjjf: With **vos** the ending takes an accent mark: **vos comés**, **vos vivís**. In Latin America, **beber** is used, but for drinks **tomar** (an -ar verb) is very common: _¿Qué tomas?_
13wyup9: Three patterns of the regular present
ok1l0z: The ella form has no accent mark: **come**. The accent mark is for _vos comés_.
jng6zu: To say how many times you do something, use a scale: **siempre** → **casi siempre** → **normalmente** → **a menudo / muchas veces** → **a veces** → **casi nunca** → **nunca**.
1imsnve: You can also be exact: **todos los días**, **todas las mañanas**, **una vez a la semana**, **dos veces al mes**. Notice the agreement: tod**os** los días, tod**as** las mañanas.
1rkedeb: Most of these expressions go before the verb or at the end of the sentence: **Siempre desayuno café** / **Desayuno café siempre**. **Todos los días** and **una vez a la semana** usually go at the end or at the beginning: **Como fruta todos los días.**
17hb6hr: **Nunca** has a special rule. Before the verb it stands alone: **Nunca bebo café.** After the verb it needs **no** in front: **No bebo nunca café.** This is the double negative: in Spanish it is correct and required.

15az1vi: If _nunca_ goes first, it doesn't need _no_.
d6s1yi: If _nunca_ goes after the verb, the verb needs **no** in front.

iuua6m: The names change by country. In many Latin American countries, **el almuerzo** is the midday meal. In Spain **la comida** is more usual. In Mexico, **la comida** is the main meal of the afternoon and **el almuerzo** can be a late breakfast, in mid-morning.
3y6nip: Many foods have regional variants: **jugo** (Latin America) / **zumo** (Spain); **papa** (Latin America, Canary Islands) / **patata** (Spain); **frijoles** (Mexico, Central America) / **porotos** (Southern Cone) / **caraotas** (Venezuela). kps10m: B and V: a single sound
1e4svg3: In modern Spanish, **b** and **v** are pronounced exactly the same. _Vino_ and _bino_ would sound identical: the difference is only in spelling. Don't pronounce the **v** with your teeth on your lip, as in English.
1zfau: That single sound has two variants depending on position. After a pause and after **m** or **n**, the lips close completely: it's a **strong [b]**, as in _**V**ino, por favor_, _u**n v**aso_, _ta**mb**ién_.
2g0sc7: In other positions —especially between vowels— the lips almost touch, but don't close: it's a **soft [β]**, as in _la **v**erdura_, _be**b**o_, _Cu**b**a_. The air passes between the lips.
16hxowo: What matters: the variant depends on the **position**, not on the letter. The same word changes: _**v**aso_ (strong, at the beginning) → _el **v**aso_ (soft).
naben4: Since they sound the same, **b** and **v** are learned with the written word. Two clues: after **m** it's always written **b** (_también, hambre_) and after **n** always **v** (_invitar, enviar_). The past-tense endings **-aba** and words with **bl, br** take **b**.
w8d4qn: The first **b** is strong (after a pause); the other two, between vowels, are soft: don't close your lips completely.
17e37ju: _Un vaso_ → «umbaso»: the **n** almost becomes **m** and the **v** is strong. _De vino_: soft.
94y7gm: _Cenamos **v**erduras_: after **s**, soft. No **v** with the teeth.
dss1co: _En **P**uebla_ is a different letter; in _be**b**emos_, the second **b** is soft.
